Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For a 45-year-old female auditor with combat trauma, 'Pregnancy/Birth Reminders' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items and downstream threat items center on hypervigilance, pursuit, and danger cues, whereas this item implies a reproductive/perinatal trigger theme that is not supported by the memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy content. It looks disconnected from the combat-based formulation rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict Eating' is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The dominant clinical pattern across triggers, threat, memory, and appraisals is fear-based hypervigilance and fragmented trauma memory, with maladaptive strategies of avoidance and rumination fitting that pattern. Restrictive eating instead suggests a separate control/body-management coping style that is not reflected elsewhere in the selected items, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same combat-related PTSD profile.

vignette: Two decades earlier, during a combat deployment, the desert heat shattered with a concussive blast that left Samira disoriented in the dust. The explosion had ripped through the moment, creating violent memory gaps that swallowed entire sequences of the attack. What remained were disconnected images-a radio sparking, a boot scraping gravel, a sky bruised purple-that never aligned into a coherent timeline. Because the event remained an incomplete picture, the memory fragmentation convinced her that the environment was inherently lethal, cementing a threat system that would never fully deactivate. In the months that followed, sensory cues began to dictate her waking hours. Whenever she heard a heavy bang or caught a whiff of cheap cologne in a grocery aisle, these auditory and olfactory jolts directly activated her need to constantly check her surroundings and map every exit. The sensory overload did not stay neutral; as the fragmented images resurfaced, they twisted into a ruthless narrative of guilt and self-blame. Samira began to believe she had fundamentally failed to protect her comrades, and that the disaster proved she was inherently flawed. Her body, she felt, had turned against her, firing alarm signals that kept her trapped in the past. This physiological betrayal convinced her that the environment was inherently lethal. Believing the world was a hostile place, Samira could no longer tolerate unsecured spaces. She started identifying escape routes before entering any room, a habit that quickly solidified into a rule: she only felt safe in a handful of familiar places. This rigid safety requirement meant that when she checked behind herself, the threat appraisal instantly resurfaced, pulling the fragmented memories forward again. Her hyper-vigilance also dictated her daily movements; she constantly scanned her surroundings for hidden dangers, which in turn widened the circle of places she avoided. The avoidance of open spaces only widened the circle of places she considered safe, cementing her threat beliefs. Her self-criticism drove her to rigid avoidance of open spaces and relentless counterfactual thinking, habits that carved her life into isolated compartments. Because she spent her days constructing escape routes and scanning for danger, she never allowed herself to process the original trauma, which only sharpened the memory gaps and hardened her negative self-appraisals. Her conviction that her body was a traitor made every cologne scent or sudden bang feel catastrophic, which directly reinforced her need to check behind herself and plot retreats. This self-reproach deepened her conviction that she was morally culpable and that the world remained fundamentally unsafe. The cycle tightened relentlessly: her appraisal that she was fundamentally flawed drove her to rigid avoidance of open spaces and relentless counterfactual thinking, habits that carved her life into isolated compartments. Because she spent her days constructing escape routes and scanning for danger, she never allowed herself to process the original trauma, which only sharpened the memory gaps and hardened her negative self-appraisals. The avoidance, in turn, stripped her of her marriage, as her ex-husband could not navigate her constant surveillance. At forty-five, the American-born auditor of Middle Eastern descent finally came to the clinic after a routine site audit triggered a panic attack that left her shaking behind a client's reception desk. Her PCL-5 score of 80 reflected the severity of a presentation that had quietly eroded her career and relationships. She was terrified that she might never reclaim her life, yet she clung to the quiet hope that someone might finally show her how to dismantle the fortress she had built around herself.
